title: A longer look and a search while the toy is still hidden are different questions
summary: Moore and Meltzoff argue that longer looking judges a visible outcome after the fact, while search aims at the object while it is still hidden.
body: Moore and Meltzoff write that looking-time studies usually compare the scene after hiding with what came before, so the infant is watching a visible outcome either way. Search, they say, can begin while the object is still hidden, and so it asks where the infant expects the hidden object to be. They offer the split to explain how the two measures can disagree. The split is their argument in the 2008 paper. It does not award every study to one side.

sources.title: Factors affecting infants' manual search for occluded objects and the genesis of object permanence
sources.author: M. Keith Moore and Andrew N. Meltzoff
sources.note: Supports their contrast: looking time as post-diction of a visible outcome, manual search as prediction while the object remains hidden.
